overview.body:
**Matsya** (*matsya*) ​— The ‌Fish, First ‌Avatāra of ​Viṣṇu · ​'The Fish' ​— the ​first avatāra ​of Viṣṇu, who ‌saved Manu ​and the ​Vedas from ‌the great ​deluge — ‌belongs to ​the Sanskrit ‌tradition, where it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Fish ​Avatar of ​Vishnu". The ‌name means ​"'The Fish' ‌— the first ​avatāra of ‌Viṣṇu, who ​saved Manu ‌and the ​Vedas from ‌the great ​deluge"[^1].

**Matsya** ​is Vishnu’s first ‌descent: the ‌great fish ‌that warned ​Manu of ​the coming ‌flood, bade ​him build ​a ship, and ‌bore it ​— and ​with it ‌the seven ​sages, the ‌seeds of ​every species, ​and the Vedas ​themselves — ​through the ‌drowning of ‌the world ​to the ‌one un-submerged ​peak. The ​Purāṇic telling makes ‌him the ‌keeper of ‌the scriptures ‌as well ​as the ‌race.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as **Matsya** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/matsya/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form — ​a description ​computed from the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *matsya* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**मत्स्य**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"'The ‌Fish' ​— the ​first ‌avatāra ​of Viṣṇu, ‌who ​saved ‌Manu and ​the ​Vedas ​from the ​great ​deluge"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*matsya* ​survives only ‌because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system ‌could ​not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ‌is a ‌technological ​compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Matsya** ​recovers the ‌full ​diacritic detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ​in ‌the address ‌bar. ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**m** → ​**M** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ‌**t** ​→ **t** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**s** → ​**s** ‌— ‌Same
- **y** ​→ ​**y** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ˈmɑːtsyə/** ​— ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Matsya).[^1]

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Mat-** — ​Short ‌a ​as ‌in “cup”; ​the ​word ​is the ​common ​noun ‌“fish”.
- ​**-sya** — ‌The ​cluster ‌tsy is ​pronounced ‌“chya” ​in ‌the north, ​“tsya” ​in ‌the south: ‌MAT-chyuh.
- ‌**** ​— ​The first ‌avatāra ​of ​Vishnu — ‌the ​fish ​that ‌saved Manu ​from ‌the ​flood.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the closest ‌approximation ​is: ‌“MAHT-chyuh”

​Kindred and ​historical ‌forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ‌**Parallels** ​— ‌Gilgamesh’s Utnapishtim ​· ​Noah ​· Deucalion
- ‌**Lineage** ​— ​first ​of the ‌daśāvatāra, ​the ​ten descents

​The ‌flood-saviour ​as ‌fish: the ​oldest ‌of ​Vishnu’s descents, ‌and ‌the ​closest ​of India’s ​myths ​to ‌the world’s ‌other ​flood-legends.

domains.body:
**Matsya** ​is Vishnu’s ‌first descent: ‌the ​great fish ​that warned ​Manu ​of the ​coming flood, ‌bade ​him build ​a ship, ‌and bore ​it ‌— and ​with it ‌the ​seven sages, ​the seeds ​of ​every species, ​and the ‌Vedas ​themselves — ‌through the ​drowning ‌of the ​world to ‌the ​one un-submerged ‌peak. The ​Purāṇic ​telling makes ‌him the ‌keeper of ‌the ​scriptures as ​well as ‌the ​race.[^1]

### The ​Great Fish

‌A ​tiny fish ​that outgrew ‌every ​vessel, until ‌only the ​ocean ​could hold ​it — ​Vishnu ‌himself.

### The ‌Deluge

The ​pralaya, ‌the world’s ​dissolution by ​water — ‌the ‌flood that ‌ends each ‌cycle ​of creation.

### ‌The Ship ​of ​Manu

The ​ark of ‌Hindu ​myth: the ​seven sages ​and ‌the seeds ​of all ​life ​aboard, tied ‌to the ​fish’s ‌horn.

### Keeper ​of the ‌Vedas

The ​demon ‌Hayagrīva stole ‌the scriptures; ​the ​fish slew ​him and ​returned ‌the Vedas ‌to the ​world.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Matsya ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The Great ​Fish** ​— ​A ​tiny ‌fish that ​outgrew ‌every ​vessel, ‌until ​only the ‌ocean ​could ‌hold ​it ​— Vishnu ‌himself.
- ‌**The ‌Deluge** ​— ​The pralaya, ‌the ​world’s ​dissolution ‌by ​water — ​the ‌flood ​that ‌ends each ​cycle ​of ​creation.
- ​**The ‌Ship of ‌Manu** ​— ‌The ​ark ​of Hindu ‌myth: ‌the ‌seven ‌sages ​and the ‌seeds ​of ​all ​life ‌aboard, tied ​to ​the ​fish’s ‌horn.
- ​**Keeper of ​the ​Vedas** ‌— ​The ‌demon Hayagrīva ​stole ‌the ​scriptures; ‌the ‌fish slew ​him ​and ​returned ​the ‌Vedas to ‌the ​world.

mythology.body:
The Matsya ​myth is India’s ‌flood-saga: the warning, the ‌ark, the world’s ​drowning, and the ​mooring at the ​one remaining peak — ​with the added ​theology of the ‌avatāra, Vishnu descending ​to preserve both species ​and scripture. The ‌telling grows from ​a brief Vedic episode ‌to one of ​the Purāṇas’ most ‌beloved complete narratives.[^1]

### ​The Earliest Flood (Śatapatha ​Brāhmaṇa)

The oldest ​telling is dry ​and swift: Manu ​finds a tiny fish, ‌rears it through ​successively larger vessels ‌until only the ​sea will hold it; ‌it warns him ​of the coming ‌flood and returns ​as a horned leviathan ‌to tow his ​ship by a ​cable. At the ‌flood’s peak they moor ‌on the one ‌un-submerged tree — ​the *nyagrodha* — and ​the fish reveals ‌itself as ‘the ​lord of creatures’.[^2]

### ​The Full Narrative (Matsya ‌Purāṇa)

The eponymous ​Purāṇa expands everything: ​the demon Hayagrīva ‌steals the four Vedas ​as Brahmā sleeps; ‌Vishnu wakes as ​a fish, kills ​Hayagrīva in the world-river’s ​depths, and returns ​the scriptures; then ‌the flood proper ‌— the ark, the ​sages, the seeds, ‌and the long ​tow to the Himalayan ​peak where the ‌new world begins.

### ‌The First Descent ‌(Avatāra Theology)

In the ‌daśāvatāra sequence, Matsya ​is the first: ‌preservation precedes power. ​The theology reads each ​avatāra as the ​god’s answer to ‌a cosmic emergency ​— here, the emergency ​is knowledge itself, ​the Vedas drowned ‌or stolen. The ​fish saves the texts ​before it saves ​the species.

### One ‌Deluge, Many Arks ​(Comparative Flood)

The flood-list ‌is the world’s ​most widespread myth-complex: ‌Utnapishtim in the Gilgamesh ​epic, Noah in ‌Genesis, Deucalion in ‌Greece, and Manu ​in the Purāṇas. The ​Indian telling’s distinctive ​signature is the ​*warning fish* — ‌the saviour who speaks, ‌and the god ​who tows.

vedic-references.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Matsya. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with fish avatar of vishnu.

The IAST restoration Matsya marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]

upanishads.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Matsya appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Matsya carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]

puranas.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Matsya in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Matsya is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]

mantras.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Matsya encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Matsya preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
